extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and weighing objective evidence (secondary considerations) when determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including standards for unexpected results, commercial success, expert opinion, nexus, comparisons to prior art, burden of proof, and commensurability with claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence must be supported by actual proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence which must be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be of probative value includes evidence of unexpected results, commercial success, solution of a long-felt need, inoperability of the prior art, invention before the date of the reference, and allegations that the author(s) of the prior art derived the disclosed subject matter from the inventor or at least one joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “It is well settled that unexpected results must be established by factual evidence.” (In re De Blauwe). Examples of statements that are not evidence and must be supported by affidavit/declaration include unexpected results, commercial success, solution of long-felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before date of reference, and derivation allegations. See MPEP § 2145 for related case law on rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant arguments cannot take the place of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments presented by the applicant are not a substitute for factual evidence in the record and therefore cannot alone carry probative weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Schulze; In re De Blauwe. Statements that are merely argument (e.g., assertions of unexpected results without tests) are deemed mere argument. Examiners should require affidavits/declarations for factual support. See MPEP § 2145 for rebuttal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of opinion evidence (expert testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert opinion testimony may be considered and given some weight so long as the opinion is not on the ultimate legal conclusion; the underlying factual basis for the opinion may be persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opinion on the ultimate legal issue is not entitled to weight, but facts supporting the opinion are. Consider the nature of the matter, the strength of opposing evidence, the expert’s interest in the outcome, and the presence/absence of factual support (Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins). Cases: In re Chilowsky; In re Lindell; In re Beattie; Ex parte George. Conclusory, unsupported expert statements have little value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting commercial success or long-felt need where blocking patent or market power exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of commercial success or long-felt need may be given less weight if record shows the applicant or patent owner has strong market power or there exists a 'blocking patent' that could have deterred others from practicing the later invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A blocking patent may explain lack of development by others; the magnitude of its deterrent effect is fact-specific. Examiners should be aware of blocking patents' potential impact and must articulate any discounting of secondary considerations in Office actions (Acorda Therapeutics v. Roxane Lab.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant timely submits evidence traversing a rejection, the examiner must reconsider patentability and weigh all competent rebuttal evidence against the evidence supporting the prima facie case; ultimate determination is by a preponderance of the entire record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each piece of rebuttal evidence is not evaluated only for its ability to knock down the prima facie case individually; all rebuttal evidence taken as a whole is weighed against the prima facie evidence (In re Oetiker; In re Piasecki). If examiner remains unconvinced, next Office action should state that and identify reasons, and explain any individual weights assigned to different objective indicia (Volvo Penta v. Brunswick). See MPEP § 2145 for sufficiency guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be shown (difference in kind vs degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in properties between the claimed invention and prior art must be unexpected (a difference in kind) rather than merely differences in degree; the issue is whether properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Merck; In re Waymouth; In re Wagner; Ex parte Gelles. A 'difference of degree' is generally less persuasive than a 'difference in kind.' Evidence must show a marked improvement or new property dissimilar to the known property to be persuasive (UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater-than-expected results and synergism as evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that results are greater than expected — including additive or synergistic effects greater than the sum of components — can be an evidentiary factor pertinent to nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corkhill: additive result persuasive where diminished result expected. Synergism may show unexpectedness (Merck v. Biocraft). However, greater-than-additive effects are not necessarily sufficient — applicants must show results exceed expectations from prior art and are of significant, practical advantage (Ex parte The NutraSweet Co.; Ex parte The NutraSweet example where prior art led to expectation of greater-than-additive effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a property shared with prior art can rebut prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the claimed compound or invention is unexpectedly superior in a property it shares with the prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness even if superiority is shown only for some uses or species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No set number of examples required (In re Chupp). Examples: improved herbicidal control for specific crops was sufficient even when average on others. See Ex parte A and related decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property as evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating the claimed invention lacks a property that would have been expected based on prior art teachings can be evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: absence of beta-adrenergic blocking activity where prior art taught such activity (Ex parte Mead Johnson). See MPEP § 2145 discussion of latent properties and additional advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and explain data
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants bear the burden to establish that differences in results are unexpected and of both statistical and practical significance, and to explain proffered data in any declaration offered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusions are not entitled to weight (Ex parte Gelles; Ex parte C). '[A]ppellants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration they proffer' (Ex parte Ishizaka). Direct and indirect comparative tests commensurate in scope with claims are probative (In re Boesch; In re Blondel; In re Fouche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons must be made with the closest prior art (and deviations explained)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to effectively rebut a prima facie case; comparisons should identify the number and relative importance of claim limitations in common and explain deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use method of comparing claim limitations to each cited reference to find closest reference (In re Merchant). Deviations from examples should be explained (In re Finley; In re Armstrong). Applicants may compare to prior art closer than that relied on by the examiner (In re Holladay).

rubrics_metrics.name: When two equally close references exist, testing one may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut prima facie obviousness unless the teachings of the references are sufficiently similar that testing one provides the same information as to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Johnson: if applicant tests fewer than all cited compounds, the testing must be sufficient to permit conclusions about relative effectiveness across the closest prior art; applicant need not test all compounds but must provide adequate basis for conclusions (quoting In re Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The showing of unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims offered to be supported — results should occur over the entire claimed range or be supported by sufficient testing to justify extrapolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to broad ranges/genera require evidence across the claimed scope or sufficient trend data from species/narrower ranges (In re Clemens; In re Peterson; In re Grasselli; In re Hill; In re Kollman). Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range requires tests both inside and outside the range to show criticality; species data can support a genus only where an artisan could reasonably infer a trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages not disclosed in the specification may still be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; the totality of the record, including proffered evidence during prosecution, is relevant to the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not contain the asserted advantage for it to be considered (In re Chu). Undisclosed inherent properties that flow from use should be considered (In re Zenitz; Ex parte Sasajima). Specification need not disclose proportions/values as critical for applicant to later present evidence of criticality (In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of production for commercial success and nexus lies with applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success must produce hard evidence of commercial success and establish a legally and factually sufficient nexus between that success and the claimed invention so the evidence is probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on applicant to provide evidence because the Office lacks means to gather it. The term 'nexus' designates a factually and legally sufficient connection between commercial success evidence and the claimed invention (Demaco v. Von Langsdorff). Commercial success abroad is relevant. See MPEP §§ 716.01(b) and 2145 for nexus guidance and supporting cases (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen).
